hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever finally gotten the thing you wanted, and then wanted the next thing?
options: me too. this king might make you smile. listen.
then you know this thirst. listen.
that’s rare, and lovely. this one is still worth keeping.

steps.line: Long ago, an old tale says, lived King Mandhata. At a touch of his hands, jewels rained from the sky, piling up knee-deep.
He ruled the whole earth. He had everything a person could want. Still, something in him leaned toward more.

steps.q: A king who owns the whole earth. What do you think he does next?
o: Conquers the sea kingdoms of the nagas
Climbs to the heavens of the gods
Searches for a way to live forever
steps.why: Up he goes, to the heavens. The thirst doesn’t stop at the edge of the world.

steps.line: So he rose to the heavens. There Sakka, king of the gods, welcomed him and shared half his throne.
For ages he ruled half of heaven. Then one thought arrived: “Why only half? I want it all.”

steps.q: He has half of heaven, and he wants the rest. What happens?
o: He plots against Sakka for the throne
The thought alone makes him fall
Sakka hands him the whole throne
steps.why: He never lifts a finger. In the Jataka, the wanting thought alone drains his power, and he drops back to earth.

steps.line: With that thought, his power left him. He fell back to earth, an old man, in his own garden.

steps.q: In the Jataka, Mandhata shared heaven’s throne so long that thirty-six Sakkas came and went. What does that detail add?
o: Even endless time didn’t quench the thirst
Sakka kept losing his throne to him
The gods were weak back then
steps.why: Age after age of heaven, and the thirst was still there. Time doesn’t fill it any more than gold does.

steps.line: Before he died, he told the people: “I had treasure, the earth and half of heaven, and it was never enough.”

steps.q: The verse about a rain of coins is in the Dhammapada. Who does it say truly follows the Buddha?
o: One who never feels a wish
One who owns nothing at all
One who delights in thirst ending
steps.why: Dhammapada 186–187: not even heavenly pleasures delight the Buddha’s disciple, who delights in the end of craving. Not wishless, not penniless: free of the thirst.

steps.line: Today, a slow line at the store. The jaw tightens. The line isn’t hurting anyone. The wanting it to be different is.
steps.label: today

say: the buddha named where the wobble comes from: tanha. it literally means thirst. he named three: thirst for pleasant things, thirst to be something, and thirst to make something go away.

and not every wish is thirst. wishing to be kind, or to help, is welcome. the trouble is the grip: “this must be different, right now.” that’s closer to home than the world is, so it’s something you can work with.

steps.q: Match each thirst to an everyday moment.
pairs: checking the fridge again, not hungry
rehearsing the comeback in the shower
thirst to make it go away
steps.why: Even wanting an unpleasant moment gone is a kind of thirst. That’s the third one, and it shows up in every slow line.

steps.q: If the wobble came from the world, more gold would fix it. What does Mandhata’s story suggest instead?
o: Find a kingdom big enough to satisfy
The work is with the thirst, not the gold
Desire is bad, so wish for nothing
steps.why: That’s the hopeful part. You can’t make every line fast, but you can work with the thirst. And wishes like kindness aren’t thirst at all.

today.say: next time you’re waiting today, in a line or for a reply, find the wanting in your body: the jaw, the chest, the hands. don’t chase it and don’t fight it. just notice: thirst.
options: one thirsty moment, noticed. that’s enough.
it will be there when you look. it always is.

tomorrow.title: The lamp that went out
tomorrow.line: a woman who has lost everything watches one small lamp go out, and is free.
